📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, method dressing for press tours is part of the reason 2026’s year of movies feels so unstoppable. The carpets for the latest Hunger Games film, Sunrise on the Reaping, have been heating up look after look, but no one is catching fire quite like Mckenna Grace. Along with her stylist, Molly Dickson, the pair have been turning out absolute masterpieces, with extraordinary commitment to Hunger Games literary lore: As small as ladybugs in Mckenna’s hair (a nod to the ‘Ladybug, Ladybug’ song Haymitch Abernathy sings to Maysilee Donner in Sunrise on the Reaping) to step out in NYC, and as large as a recreation of Katniss’s truly iconic wedding dress from The Hunger Games 2: Catching Fire.

“Mckenna was absolutely certain from the beginning that she wanted to embrace method dressing for this press tour, and I was completely on board,” Molly tells Cosmopolitan.

Recent findings suggest that the concept of method dressing isn’t latest, but it’s been incredibly impactful on movie press runs in particular over the past few years. In practice, actors wear looks that reference niche details of the films they’re promoting. Think Zendaya’s Greek-goddess-forward looks for The Odyssey, Margot Robbie’s Barbie ensembles pulled straight from the dolls themselves, Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo in a lifetime’s worth of pink and green for Wicked.

Industry observers note that “I think the best method dressing moments are the ones that tell a story, while still feeling like incredible fashion looks of their own,” notes Molly. “We wanted the fans to have those moments of recognition and excitement, but we also wanted someone who knew nothing about The Hunger Games to look at Mckenna and simply think she looked incredible!”.

Recent findings suggest that so how did they do it? What references were on their mood board? What dress almost never saw the light of day? And most importantly: What’s the story behind THE legendary arena dress from the UK premiere? Superstar stylist Molly Dickson answers our most pressing press tour related questions.

In a recent development, it was a really collaborative process between the two of us. Mckenna would come to me with ideas, and I would figure out how to translate them into fashion. She was the one who remarked, ‘Ladybugs are part of the movie, we need to do a ladybug look!’ From there, I started sourcing pieces that either incorporated ladybugs directly or finding more unexpected, interesting ways to reference them.

We were very intentional about making sure every look had a connection to some part of the Hunger Games universe. We wanted the references to feel thoughtful and recognizable to the fans, while still creating beautiful fashion moments that felt authentic to Mckenna and her personal style.

Industry observers note that I don't think either of us initially realized just how invested the Hunger Games fans would be in all the little references and Easter eggs! Once we started seeing that reaction, it became more fun to dig deeper into the franchise and pull inspiration from different characters and iconic moments. Mckenna knows this world so well, and I loved being able to bring her ideas to life.

Mckenna really wanted to pay homage to the strong female characters throughout the franchise—specifically Katniss and Joanna Mason—which became the inspiration for so many of our looks. As we started fittings, we found ways to incorporate inspiration from Rue as well.

Industry observers note that we wanted a mix of more recognizable references and subtle nods rather than exact recreations of costumes from the movies. We used the original costumes and characters as our starting point, but then put our own fashion interpretation on them. I think that's where my creativity really comes in. You want fans to recognize the inspiration, but you also want the looks to feel fresh, elevated, and true to the person wearing them.

Recent findings suggest that I really can't think of a better way to generate excitement and conversation around a movie through fashion than method dressing. It's such a fun way to bring the story beyond the screen, and give fans something deeper to connect with. What I loved most about this tour was seeing the conversations happening online, not just about the fashion itself, but about the characters, the references, and ultimately the film.

I think my personal favorite was Mckenna’s Paris look inspired by Katniss's wedding gown. It was such a major fashion moment—we actually went back and forth on whether it might be too much! Mckenna’s team really encouraged us to go for it, and they were absolutely right.

Recent findings suggest that the most challenging part was figuring out how to recreate the sculptural silver elements. Michael Ngo made experimental custom silver pieces for us, which we paired with a beautiful vintage Monique Lhuillier wedding gown. I loved that the complete look felt like a true tribute to Katniss's iconic gown, but still had its own fashion identity. It was one of those moments where the creativity, collaboration, and a little bit of risk-taking really paid off!

We really wanted to pay homage to the strong female characters throughout the Hunger Games franchise while still staying true to Mckenna's personal style. We wanted each look to tell a story and have a connection to the films, but never feel like she was wearing a costume.

For the press junkets and more casual appearances, we focused on subtle nods to the movies, whether that was through color, texture, or small details that fans might recognize. For the bigger red carpet moments, we had the opportunity to be a little more dramatic and lean into those bigger, more established references. The fun of this tour was finding that balance between fashion and storytelling!

Honestly, I have to give all the credit to Mckenna’s mom for this one! She actually discovered the dress on Instagram and sent it over to me. The brand is ALmée, and they’re based in Vietnam.

Sources indicate that I love that this look came together in such an unexpected way. It wasn't something we had custom-designed or planned months in advance. It was really just Mckenna's mom spotting something incredible and all of us realizing how perfectly it fit into the Hunger Games world.

That's one of my favorite things about styling: Sometimes the most exciting looks come from the most unexpected places, and this was definitely one of those moments!

In a recent development, one of the looks I was most excited about, but also the most stumped on creatively, Katniss's iconic Girl on Fire gown. The challenge was figuring out how to translate that moment into something that felt like a beautiful red carpet gown rather than a costume.

Sources indicate that cong Tri immediately came to mind because of their intricate beadwork and craftsmanship. I knew I wanted the fire gown to incorporate beading because of the way it catches the light, especially under red carpet lighting and camera flashes. I felt that was going to be key to creating the illusion of flames and bringing the dress to life.

It was honestly the perfect collaboration. The Cong Tri team was so willing to push the design creatively. After experimenting with different fabrics, textures, and techniques, the end result was exactly what we had hoped for. The dress felt dramatic and powerful, with that obvious nod to Katniss, but still felt like a really beautiful fashion moment. That's always the goal with these kinds of looks!

Quilted Liner Jackets Are the Swerve Your Wardrobe Needs. Here Are 10 Stellar Picks.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Layering is the name of the game in fall and winter.
  • A good tee certainly isn’t going anywhere, nor is a sweater.
  • Once upon a time, these padded jackets served as the interior protective shell worn under World War II era flight jackets before expanding into more mainstream outerwear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Layering is the name of the game in fall and winter. For the next few months, you are not a person; you’re a living, breathing Russian nesting doll. You are encased in strategic layers of t-shirts, sweaters, scarves, light jackets, and major jackets that you divest yourself of over the course of a day (or night). Like a knight donning his armor, you will spend this season dutifully putting on and taking off each of these individual pieces as you fight the seemingly endless battle against winter.

A few pieces are a given. A good tee certainly isn’t going anywhere, nor is a sweater. The specific kind of Significant Coat you use varies depending on the guy and his style, but it’s nevertheless a guaranteed winter staple. Those middle layers can be a bit of a toss up, though, which is how you might encounter something like a quilted liner jacket.

Once upon a time, these padded jackets served as the interior protective shell worn under World War II era flight jackets before expanding into more mainstream outerwear. The quilted padding traps body heat, but doesn’t make the jacket so heavy that it just feels like another cumbersome layer. You can still wear it as a liner jacket—but lowkey, if it’s the right temperature, they also work pretty well on their own. So if you’re in the market for a new versatile transitional weather jacket, you’ve come to the right place.

Sources indicate that if we had to pick one from this entire group, it would be this jacket from Buck Mason ... And it’s really not that close. Inspired by old-school mountaineering outfits, the nylon is woven in Japan, and the down fill has an exceptional warmth rating. Add a elastic cuffs and a fit that works layered underneath or overtop, it’s perfect.

Look, layering’s great and all—but no one talks about how annoying and awkward it is when you get hot enough to take off one layer, but then are stuck just kind of holding onto it until you get the chance to put it down or hang it up. That’s not a problem with this packable Paul Smith shirt jacket. Let it do its magic to keep you warm. When you’re ready to take it off, simply collapse it down, zip it up, and stuff it away into your pocket until you need it again.

Industry observers note that rains has a well-established reputation of balancing fashion and function with their outerwear, whether it’s their Esquire-editor favorite Fishtail Parka or this bomber liner jacket. Nothing beats a classic leather bomber...except maybe the rain (leather + rain = no bueno). That’s not an issue with Rains’ Banja bomber liner. You get that same edgy look, but with a slightly more practical construction. Plus there’s something sleekly minimal about the channel quilting. Layer it beneath your actual bomber or heavy coat of choice for optimal warmth all season long.

Look, we love a good Dickies moment. They make some of our favorite pants of all time, not least of which because they’re mad affordable—though that’s a pretty major element to it. So naturally, if someone comes up to us asking for a high-quality and stylish quilted liner jacket at well under $100, we’ve got one word for ya: Dickies.

Barbour’s been making sturdy outerwear that can withstand the rainy U.K. weather since the 1800s. And while they don’t strictly make a liner jacket, this lightweight—or “Flyweight,” as Barbour calls it—quilted jacket gets pretty close.

With a sleek, collarless design, this Fieldworth jacket can easily slide under any heavy coat. It falls more into “middleweight jacket” territory, meaning it’ll probably keep you toastier than some of the other options on this list—both on its own and when layered up.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for more of a typical fall/spring jacket, J.Crew’s PrimaLoft® jacket is where it’s at. The quintessentially Americana brand uses the down alternative to create a well-insulated transitional weather jacket you can layer with, or wear on its own.

Look, all these other brands and designers are great and all—but Alpha Industries is the real deal. No like seriously. When the company was first founded in Tennessee in the 1950s, it was as a clothing contractor for the United States Department of Defense. These were the guys making those sexy flight jackets long before Tom Cruise shrugged one on in Top Gun. Their Deco Liner nods to the OG liners of yore, featuring a slim, collarless design that will integrate with additional layers. Wear the jacket by itself when you start feeling warmer, and let the whole world see the Alpha embroidery on the back so everyone knows this is some top of line shit.

According to recent reports, if you’re in the market for something lighter and less padded, opt for this cotton hunting jacket. The silhouette takes inspiration from vintage Czech military liners and traditional hunting gear to create a layer of outerwear breezy but still warm.

Get two jackets for the price of one with this reversible number from Cos. You get all the benefits of a quilted coat, with the versatile sleekness of a classic collarless jacket.

#43387. Take Note: This Is How Cool People Are Decorating for Thanksgiving This Year

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2472 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

Take Note: This Is How Cool People Are Decorating for Thanksgiving This Year

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor.
  • Pumpkin centerpieces, rustic garlands, dried-fruit wreaths, and cornucopias are classic Thanksgiving decorations.
  • From traditional touches to wholly unexpected looks, read on to see how they’re making their homes feel festive this autumn, and maybe you’ll be inspired to try something new this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Pumpkin centerpieces, rustic garlands, dried-fruit wreaths, and cornucopias are classic Thanksgiving decorations. They’re timeless and beloved, but they can also feel predictable. Traditional decor has its place, of course, but Thanksgiving tablescapes—and dinner parties in general—are evolving, much like interiors, to feel more personal, lived-in, and layered. So we asked nine tastemakers and experts how they’re decorating for this family-centric holiday.

From traditional touches to wholly unexpected looks, read on to see how they’re making their homes feel festive this autumn, and maybe you’ll be inspired to try something new this year.

Ever since designer Mikel Welch moved to sunny California, his family has never hesitated to go to his for Thanksgiving to escape the chilly Michigan weather. It’s become a tradition to gather at his house, and similarly to how he grew up, Welch likes to keep his decorations for the holiday understated and warm.

“I love getting the exterior of my house into full fall mode with mums, pumpkins, and seasonal greenery,” Welch tells House Beautiful. “The beauty of fall decorating is that it can carry you from October straight through Thanksgiving without having to change much.”.

The designer’s house is filled with dark, moody colors and earthy textures year-round, so he focuses mainly on bringing natural elements inside to do the work for him. “I also have a little tradition with my dad,” he adds. “For the past couple of years, we've made trips to the nursery together to pick out flowers, greenery, and sometimes bales of hay for the front of the house. It's become something I really enjoy doing with him.”.

“Thanksgiving has always been a major family affair,” real estate expert and maximalism extraordinaire Harvin Greene says. She’s happy to keep that tradition going as an adult, just in her own way. In the past, Greene’s aunt and uncle would have everyone at their house for the big meal, but last year, they passed the hosting baton to Greene for the first time. “I may have gotten a little carried away...in the best possible way.”.

Sources indicate that getting to decorate two tables—one for the “adults,” another for the “kids,” even though they’re technically all grown-ups, too—Greene used this opportunity to design two completely different tablescapes. “I grew up surrounded by women who understood that a beautifully set table and a genuinely good time should go hand in hand,” she adds.

Sources indicate that the one in the formal dining space (i.e., the “adults’” table) was theatrical and dramatic, and nearly everything on it had some sort of familial connection, from her parents’ engraved goblets to her husband’s grandmother’s sterling flatware. The kids’ table, on the other hand, was whimsical and vibrant, complete with a yellow patterned tablecloth, colorful glassware, and playful animal candlesticks. “I don't feel the need to follow the traditional Thanksgiving color palette,” Greene says. “Who decided Thanksgiving had to be orange and brown? Yellow, pink, turquoise, and green can be just as festive.”.

It has been revealed that the holiday isn’t over until they bring out the Bingo cards, a spirited Thanksgiving tradition that Greene’s Aunt Jean started—which involves cash prizes. “It's one of those family traditions that makes the holiday feel like ours, no matter whose house we're celebrating in.”.

Talia Hubble is no stranger to a good dinner party—much of her content actually centers around her love of hosting. But Thanksgiving is a bit extra special for the Rhode Islander, especially since it’s being held at her cottage this year. “Growing up, it was just me and my mom, and she was too busy to decorate,” Hubble notes. “I think that’s part of why I’ve fallen in love with seasonal decorating as an adult, I get to bring all my cozy childhood decorating dreams to life!”.

Recent findings suggest that as soon as the calendar switches from October to November, Hubble starts decorating for fall, opting for an eclectic mix of subtle Christmas decor (think bows, garlands, and wreaths), an excessive amount of taper candles, and a traditional Thanksgiving palette of oranges, browns, greens, and reds. Every year looks a little bit different, but there are pieces in her collection that are simply too cute not to bring out every holiday season.

Industry observers note that “Half the fun of pulling everything out for Thanksgiving is remembering where it came from,” she says. “I think the best decor is a culmination of pieces you’ve been collecting for years, and the memories behind those pieces are what make the table feel special and uniquely yours.”.

According to recent reports, by the time she’s done decorating, her home feels like a warm, welcoming escape, somewhere her guests can exhale. “My philosophy is that you can’t go wrong when you aim for cozy, colorful, and embrace a little organized mess,” Hubble adds. “My favorite Thanksgiving tables are the ones that look even better halfway through dinner, when the napkins are rumpled and everyone’s reaching for seconds.”.

Chef and food stylist Romilly Newman can’t always count on being in the same place as her family for Thanksgiving since everyone’s scattered about, but she always makes a point to throw an autumnal dinner with friends around the holiday time, complete with beautiful fall decor.

Recent findings suggest that her mom never decorated their home while she was growing up with specific Thanksgiving decorations—instead, she would decorate with deep orange and red flowers to capture the fall vibe. Newman’s style as an adult is similar. “I am fall-obsessed, so as soon as the temperature drops from summer, I'm setting up branches, candles, and darker accents,” she indicates. “I love the atmosphere inside and outside around Thanksgiving time, and I try my best to bottle that up in my home.”.

Natural thicker linen, pops of silver, dark florals, and moody lighting envelop her space as the chef relies mostly on candlelight and organic elements—like figs, sage, chestnuts, and mandarins—as the decorative accents.

“Thanksgiving is great because it brings family together and offers time to enjoy food, friends, and being at home,” Newman adds. “Whatever your style is, try to create an environment that allows for great conversation and a festive evening. You want everyone to be comfortable and feel the holiday spirit.”.

Industry observers note that when writer Olivia Noceda was a child, she would stay up late the night before Thanksgiving and design custom menus for everyone on Microsoft Paint, which she would then print out, frame, and place on each table setting in preparation for the substantial meal. The holiday was a big deal for Noceda’s mother, who would always put on the most beautiful Thanksgiving gatherings. “I think that's where my love for hosting and setting a beautiful table really started,” she explains.

However, for the last six years, Noceda has been having Thanksgiving with her husband’s side of the family, so when she does host around the holiday, it’s typically for Friendsgiving. “I don't necessarily pick a theme, but I do like everything to feel cohesive,” she explains of her decorating process. “I usually start incorporating little autumnal touches sometime in October and let them carry me through Thanksgiving.”.

In a recent development, the writer and recipe developer lets the season guide her, building her tablescape and decor around a beautiful branch from the farmers’ market, a bowl of pears or persimmons, a collection of little pumpkins and squash, or a few taper candles on the dining room table. Ingredients play a big part in her decor—she can even take a fresh loaf of bread and make it feel special on her table.

For the rest of her decor, she likes to incorporate vintage serving pieces, everyday elements, and elevated details like antique silver and linen napkins with things she already owns to lean into that lived-in, warm feeling. The last thing she wants is her home to feel like a department store display. “Nothing needs to match perfectly, and I actually prefer when it doesn't,” Noceda adds.

In a recent development, what entrepreneur and Real Housewives of New York star Erin Lichy remembers best about Thanksgivings growing up is the smell. “We always spent Thanksgiving out east, and the house was full of pumpkins, local hay, and lanterns,” she explains. The scent of that fresh produce, mixed with her grandmother’s homemade turkey t’bit, has shaped the way she decorates for and hosts Thanksgiving. “That coveted and highly personal (and incredibly delicious) recipe is in my cookbook, She’s a Host, and it’s part of every Thanksgiving I host.”.

In a recent development, decorating starts in the kitchen for her family. Lichy wants the home to smell like fall, so she focuses on that sense, making seasonal recipes with squash and pumpkin and incorporating autumnal flowers in her interiors. The melding of those scents gives her townhouse a warm feeling, especially when mixed with layered fall colors and the crackling of the fireplace.

Ever since Lichy and her family have moved into their townhouse, she’s been obsessed with decorating her stoop too. “The stoop is the first thing everyone sees, so this year I decided to bring in Simon Wallace Design to make it really stand out!” Lichy adds. “They completely transformed it with layers of seasonal color and texture, and it feels so warm and welcoming.” She specifically loves using the faux garlands and pinecones, as well as lanterns, from Balsam Hill and Frontgate because they’re so beautifully made that they look real, and she’s able to reuse them year after year.

No matter what she does to decorate though, she just wants her home to feel warm and lived-in, and this is the season and holiday to really lean into that.

Decorating for the holidays is Gabby Amato’s version of a self-care day. “It's truly one of my favorite days of the year,” she says. “I carve out a weekend afternoon when my husband and son are out of the house, light my favorite fall candles, turn on some music, and have the house entirely to myself.”.

Amato, the founder of Table Two Studio, a paper plate brand which specializes in beautiful, artistic designs that you definitely won’t want to throw away, credits her love of Thanksgiving and the fall season in general to her mother. While growing up in the ‘90s, she saw her mom put so much care and effort into the holiday decorations, always making their home feel warm, nostalgic, and full of spirit. “For Thanksgiving, she decorated our mantel with gourds, greenery, and ceramic pilgrim statues that were a gift from my grandmother,” Amato states. “We had oversized cornstalks and pumpkins at the front door. Nothing ever felt overly styled or precious.”.

In a recent development, it’s this feeling that has stuck with her throughout her life, and it’s what she hopes she captures in her own home every year. She begins decorating for the fall early, right after Labor Day, pulling out old pieces and unboxing anything new and arranging it all in fresh ways so nothing feels stale. “I love beautiful decor, of course, but I'm much more interested in creating an atmosphere than achieving a particular aesthetic,” she adds. “I want my home to feel warm, lived-in, a little nostalgic, and festive.”.

Sources indicate that donna Lennard’s family was never one for holiday dressing—most of the attention at Thanksgiving fell on the delicious food shared with family. As a restauranteur and cofounder of beloved NYC establishment il Buco, it makes sense why the meal remains to be the most important thing to Lennard even today.

“Clearly, the table is always festive, whether it’s the tablecloth, the napkins, or linens that reflect the season in burnt orange and the like,” she explains. “I love to decorate a table with assorted colorful gourds and seasonal florals, beautiful candlelight (our beeswax candles already have an orange glow), orange ranunculus, and the occasional dried floral.” Colorful Pienza glassware dots the table and her plethora of beautiful tableware gives it more character, but she keeps everything else relatively simple to ensure the food remains the center of attention.

Though Lennard doesn’t often host her family and friends for the Thanksgiving meal, she’s already looking forward to next year when everyone will finally gather at her beach house.

According to recent reports, being from Australia, Kendall Knox—the cofounder of Olive Ateliers along with her husband—didn’t have a personal reference of what the holiday “should” be or look like. This gives her the freedom of deciding what it is for her family. “What it has become is an intimate table: my husband Ben, our son Rhodes, and Ben's mum,” she claims. “No rotation, no kids' table, no forty-pound bird. Just the four of us and a dinner that runs long because nobody is in a hurry to leave it.”.

Industry observers note that since Knox isn’t beholden to the classic Thanksgiving decor, she tends to keep her home and her table rather simple, “shopping the house,” as she puts it to decorate instead of buying something fresh. She keeps a rather neutral palette of rich browns, creamy whites, terracotta, and silver, then uses antique linens, mismatched silverware, and candlesticks that have collected wax to capture the true lived-in feel.

Her focus tends to be on the table and the meal, letting the food add more color. If a tablecloth has a wine ring on it from the year before, all the better—it complements the stacked plates at the end of the meal.

Recent findings suggest that “The objects that come out every year, that get a little more marked each time, are the ones that end up meaning the most,” Knox adds. “Thanksgiving is just a very good excuse to use them.”.

Above: Listed for $75 million, the Hillandale estate sits on 268 acres in Stamford, Connecticut.

HBO’s The Gilded Age is back for a fourth season, once again bringing viewers into the lavish homes where the Russell and van Rhijn families’ dramas unfold. Filmed at some of the era’s most impressive estates, the series serves up grand ballrooms, château-style manors, and sumptuous drapery in abundance. It’s enough to stir up a little real estate envy. Fortunately, three extraordinary Gilded Age homes are currently on the market, offering the chance to live out that fantasy in real life. Take a peek inside below.

Dating to the turn of the century, this lavish European-style estate—known as Hillandale—once belonged to the Sulzberger family, owners of The Upcoming York Times. Located along the Connecticut border with New York, the star of the 268-acre compound is an eight-bedroom mansion designed by architecture firm Hunt & Hunt that spans more than 15,000 square feet. Featuring elaborate millwork, moldings, plasterwork, and stained glass, the manor features plenty of amenities. Olympic-sized indoor pool? Check. Elevator? There are two. Grounds? They include formal gardens, four guest houses, a private lake, and even a hedge maze. The opulent spread is listed with Leslie McElwreath of Sotheby’s International Realty.

Recent findings suggest that an Anglo-Italianate brownstone in Upcoming York’s Chelsea Historic District, the Van Ness House was built in the mid-19th century and was later enlarged to its present 7,800-square-foot size. Revamped by ELLE Decor A-List designer Miles Redd, the seven-level landmark pays homage to its elegant roots, with preserved plaster moldings, custom millwork, elegant wallcoverings, and heated oak floors in a retro chevron pattern. In the back, a landscaped private garden is paved in limestone and dotted with linden trees that turn golden in the fall. Atop the five-bedroom townhouse, which is listed with Nick Gavin and Amber Gregory of Compass, is a rooftop garden with views of Saint Peter’s Church.

Spanning 14,100 square feet, this Beaux-Arts mansion right off Fifth Avenue was constructed in 1902 by architect James R. Turner and William G. Killian. Its interiors, meanwhile, are by John Russell Pope, the genius behind the Jefferson Memorial and the National Gallery of Art. Clad in a medley of brick, limestone, and marble, the eight-bedroom house has retained its stately proportions throughout the years, including a formal dining room lined in carved wood panels. Also inside are a trio of staircases, an elevator servicing six of the seven floors, and two rooftop terraces. It’s listed for $35 million with Brian Meier and Amanda Barba of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices.

Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As you might recall, Kate was first introduced during SLOMW season 2 as Chase McWhorter’s on-again, off-again girlfriend.
  • According to recent reports, it wasn’t until summer 2025, however, that Layla and Kate really cemented their friendship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh season of The Circle is here, but it’s not just civilians competing this time around. In the Hulu revival series, celebrities are also part of the competition, including The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Layla Taylor—though her fellow competitors don’t know that, since she’s playing as a former Mormon bisexual bro named Doug. She’s not doing it alone, either, as she entered the Circle with her bestie Kate Racker. Who is Kate, you ask? I paid a visit to her and Layla’s apartment in Atlanta to get to know her (and her SLOMW lore) a little better.

As you might recall, Kate was first introduced during SLOMW season 2 as Chase McWhorter’s on-again, off-again girlfriend. She later explained to People that she and Chase met just three weeks after she split from her ex-husband (with whom she shares a son, Rowan), and it was through Chase that she met the MomTok crew, including Layla (though fun fact: Kate already knew Jessi Draper, who was her neighbor growing up, as well as Jacob Neeley, who she used to work with in private equity).

According to recent reports, it wasn’t until summer 2025, however, that Layla and Kate really cemented their friendship. “Before she started dating Mason [McWhorter], and I was kind of off with Chase, Layla and I were just single together. So we’d go out, we talk every day,” Kate previously told People. “We were kind of each other’s person. We’d FaceTime 24/7 and just got really, really, really close.”.

Recent findings suggest that now they’re spending 24/7 together in the Circle, where—according to Kate—they’ve only gotten into “one tiny little tiff” so far. “We are sisters at this point, and I consider her my sister,” she notes, adding, “I think the thing about me and Layla is we’re both like pretty sensitive, but we both love each other so much, and we’re committed [to winning]. Like, I have goosebumps.”.

My massive question for them: Why did they decide to step into the Circle as a catfish rather than themselves?

“It’s kind of fun to like step into somebody that you’re not,” Layla indicates.

Kate agrees, adding, “It’s a new experience. I mean, we’re all about new experiences and trying new things and role play. We love role play. We’ll try anything three times.”.

And if you’re wondering whether they have a certain man (or a certain pair of brothers) in mind while playing “Doug,” the answer is...not really. “I feel like he’s kind of a collection of the men that we have encountered in our life or even dated in the past,” explains Layla. “Like, all of them.”.

“I think we’re trying to lean into the douchebag,” adds Kate. “Not to say all men are douchebags, but no, there’s some great ones. Or, you know, a few.”.

Layla then clarifies, “We’re not men haters. No, not at all. We are men observers. And we’ve observed poor behavior from the men that we do know, and we’re just emulating and dramatizing that.”.

I also ask Layla if she’s missing her girlfriend Kelsie Chesser while she’s in the Circle, and she says that—while she says, “For sure, you know, I love her dearly”—the harder part is being away from her kids. “Yeah, we both cry every day,” Layla says. “Cried myself to sleep last night. But Kate is my bestie, and there’s no one I’d rather be trapped in here with.”.

Since there are players who have yet to be revealed in the Circle, I need to know: Which of the Mormon Wives would they be most excited to see pop up on their screen?

“I would love to see Jessi,” Kate states. “Obviously, Miranda [Hope]. Miranda would be great. Mayci [Neeley]. Like, any of them.”.

Layla grins before adding, “Yeah, I think I can say everyone...but one.”.

I am what you might call a problem sleeper. I often toss and turn for hours before falling asleep. Sleep aids don’t work on me (if I’m sick and take NyQuil, I end up with insomnia rather than a deep slumber). I’ll wake up at witching hour and worry about something before falling back asleep. All of this has been known to wreak havoc on my face. After nights when I barely clock five hours, I wake up to dark circles, a duller complexion, and puffy skin. But Augustinus Bader’s The Overnight Restorative Cream works like an insurance policy for sleepless nights.

Recent findings suggest that skin repairs itself overnight, and just like every other function in your body, it doesn’t do it as well when you don’t sleep. This can lead to inflammation, a damaged barrier, and even accelerated aging (not exactly what I want to hear as a chronic insomniac). While many beauty products have promised to fake the appearance of eight hours of sleep, Augustinus Bader’s fresh cream has a unique rosehip extract that mimics the effects of melatonin. While the hormone regulates your sleep cycle, melatonin could also be good for your skin. One study even found that it might have antiaging properties thanks to its ability to protect cells. This cream is also made with both polyglutamic and hyaluronic acid to seal in hydration. There’s cica to calm skin and combat inflammation. And of course, since it’s an Augustinus Bader product, there’s also an advanced form of TFC8, the brand’s proprietary ingredient, which facilitates communication between skin cells for repair and renewal.

Recent findings suggest that since using this moisturizer, my skin looks clear, toned, and glowy most mornings. While I do look bright-eyed and bushy-tailed when I manage to sleep that long and use this cream, my skin looks just as good when I get six hours of sleep. Or—gulp—five. (Any less and my brain isn’t even functioning enough to examine the state of my skin.) My next trick will be to find a face cream that puts me to sleep, but since products can’t, at the current moment, work miracles (including this one), I’ll settle for one that helps mitigate the effects of a bad night.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, christmas is just around the corner, and as the holiday spirit makes its way into our homes, it’s a good time to give your seasonal decor a refresh.
  • However, if you’re in the mood to try something a little different, here are seven trends on our radar for a chic Christmas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pictured above: A holiday-ready space by designer Marie Flanigan.

According to recent reports, christmas is just around the corner, and as the holiday spirit makes its way into our homes, it’s a good time to give your seasonal decor a refresh. This year, on-trend doesn’t have to mean brand-fresh—designers love decorating with heirloom pieces collected over time.

However, if you’re in the mood to try something a little different, here are seven trends on our radar for a chic Christmas.

Sources indicate that this winter, our decor is taking a note from European culture—again. Swedish folk art is emerging as a hot winter trend in both holiday and home decor. Defined by bold red hues, tulip motifs, and S-scrolls, the style blends cozy-core with the heritage style craze.

“European folk influences are so significant right now,” says designer Johanna Lyle of Jo Lyle & Co. “Think Swedish Dala horses, quilt motifs, and decorative stitching. I think we will see those continue into holiday decor.”.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to her tree decor, interior designer Francesca Grace waves a hand at the carefully contrived, and she’s not alone. “My ornaments are collected from my travels, so the tree is really a collection of memories. I love unpacking them and remembering where each one came from. They don’t all match, and I wouldn’t want them to,” claims Grace. “I let the ornaments lead. That mix feels much more personal to me, and it gives the tree something new to say as the collection grows.” This year’s trends hinge on antiqued, inherited style, with one-off pieces that channel bold character and hardly ever come with a matching set.

Interior designer Marie Flanigan likes to add a fresh twist to her seasonal decor with dried oranges and pops of cranberry red.

“We've seen such a beautiful resurgence of dried citrus in holiday decorating over the past few years,” Flanigan explains. “And I think cranberries are ready for their moment to shine. Their rich red hue feels especially festive, and I love the idea of incorporating them into fresh greenery, draping them across a mantel, or pairing them with dried oranges for a more layered look.”.

If there’s one classic Christmas element Grace hopes makes a comeback, it's multicolored lights. Inherently nostalgic, these bold-hued bulbs were a ’90s staple.

Sources indicate that “I’m ready for a little less restraint on the tree. Those reds, blues, greens, and yellows immediately bring back the feeling of Christmas as a child. They also pull together a collection of ornaments that might otherwise seem completely unrelated. White lights can be beautiful, but I want my Christmas tree to have some mischief,” claims Grace.

The classic red-and-green combination may take the title for the most iconic holiday palette, but this year, color trends are going complementary. While base colors stay warm and slightly rusted, patterned pieces are taking on cooler tones. This year, we’re also trading traditional plaid for Scottish tartan.

“Warm crimsons, rich browns, tactile fabrics, and blue-green plaids make a beautiful holiday palette,” indicates Elizabeth Bennett, cofounder of the interior design firm Kobel + Co.

In a total rejection of mass-manufactured everything, handmade felt pieces are taking holiday homes by storm. The style has even coined a newly introduced holiday aesthetic: #Kitschmas, and, according to Lyle, it’s here to stay. “As AI continues to homogenize design, things made by humans will feel more special and crucial. Handmade and crafted items create stories around decor that feel meaningful and can be treasured year after year,” she notes.

Moody browns are steadily emerging as the newly introduced neutral as we inch closer to the new year, and lucky for our winter design schemes, the hue really is as versatile as it seems. Paired with powdery blues, bold crimsons, and even minty greens, chocolate brown grounds nearly any palette and matches every metallic hue.

In a recent development, “I’m particularly drawn to chocolate brown as an unexpected foundation for holiday color palettes. It's incredibly rich and versatile. I love the idea of moving beyond traditional red and green and allowing the existing colors of a room to inform the holiday decor. You can create something incredibly festive through tonal layering, subtle metallic accents, and variations in material,” Flanigan explains.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot of chatter—and, let’s face it, uncertainty—about what teen girls actually want as gifts. I track shopping trends for a living and also happen to be a mom of a Gen Z daughter, so I know how often they change their minds about what’s cool. Fortunately, my daughter is always happy to give me an honest, up-to-date report.

Industry observers note that when she graduated from high school, we wanted to get her something nice. More importantly, we wanted to get her something she really wanted. I have to admit I was surprised when she told us she wanted Longchamp’s Le Pliage tote. That’s right, that tote. The one that was all the rage in the mid-aughts.

In a recent development, “It was around 2006 when my best friends and I gifted each other Longchamp totes for our birthdays,” Deputy Managing Editor Cristina Corvino tells me. “They seemed like gold to our teen selves at the time. Who knew they'd still be coveted teen gifts 20 years later? I feel validated!”.

According to recent reports, on a practical level, getting my daughter an under-$200 designer bag turned out to be a great idea. The tote is made of water-resistant nylon with a leather handle and flap, and I like that it zips all the way shut. It has a roomy main compartment, and it sits comfortably on her shoulder. To this day, it’s the tote she carries around her college campus and the one she brings with her when she comes home to visit.

But, honestly? When I bought it, I had no idea how popular this specific tote is with teen girls. Several of her friends also have the Le Pliage, and when we dropped her off at college, I couldn’t help but notice its iconic silhouette whenever yet another college kid strolled by with one on their arm.

Industry observers note that so if you’re looking for a meaningful, decidedly grown-up gift for your stylish teen—and your wallet has grown tired of chasing one fleeting trend after another—I’m willing to bet they’d be thrilled to get a Longchamp. If they already have the Le Pliage tote (clearly, I wouldn’t be surprised), here are a few more thoughtful, under-$250 Longchamp gifts to consider.

We Really Need to Talk About the MobLand Season 2 Finale

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two seasons in, the plot has racked up more lines than Eddie put up his nose the night he stabbed Tommy Stevenson in season 1.
  • Trouble is, when you’re an anti-Midas who turns everything he touches to shit, respect is a dish that never leaves the kitchen.
  • In a recent development, mobLand opened with Eddie turning a stabbing into a gang war, so it seems fitting that we end with Eddie turning an assassination into an own goal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nothing is simple in MobLand. Two seasons in, the plot has racked up more lines than Eddie put up his nose the night he stabbed Tommy Stevenson in season 1. Actually, that’s not strictly true. One thing is simple in MobLand: Eddie. He is a simpleton of truly Homeric (as in Simpson) proportions: a smarmy, sneering, simpering Freudian mess, channelled with gimlet-eyed precision by Anson Boon. All he wants is his God-given right to be respected.

Trouble is, when you’re an anti-Midas who turns everything he touches to shit, respect is a dish that never leaves the kitchen. Eddie is, in Kevin’s words in season 1, “a knifey little twerp.” That stabbing set the whole bloody saga in motion, so it’s only right that two seasons later we end with Eddie the Incompetent. Full circle, then, like a roundabout made of corpses.

In a recent development, mobLand opened with Eddie turning a stabbing into a gang war, so it seems fitting that we end with Eddie turning an assassination into an own goal. But we’ll get to that.

It seems Conrad’s chickens are coming home to roost, and his marbles are jangling around his head like loose change. We open the episode with his card being declined at a petrol station. In frustration, he shoots the till boy dead. But he knows what it means.

Industry observers note that “We’re getting lifted,” he tells Maeve in the car. Police are raiding the entire business: bank accounts are frozen, warrants are out, and Tattersall is telling reporters the Harrigans have links to terror groups across the globe. The family convenes at a dingy old safe house out of town.

In a recent development, “We’re terrorists,” says Seraphina. “We’re looking at life in Guantánamo. It’s now or never.”.

Sources indicate that her initiative has been bubbling for a while. She calls it Harrigan 2.0: going global.

Industry observers note that remember the diplomatic suitcase of diamonds Seraphina collected from her billionaire stepdad Charlton in the last episode? It was meant to fund her and Bella’s takeover of the Harrigan operation. Now, it seems, Harry has it. He takes her aside to let her know he knows. “How did you know?” she asks, incredulous.

Then he states the three words he says more than any others in MobLand: “It’s my job.”.

Inside the safe house, the family are all there, and everyone has a initiative to pitch. Kevin wants to crawl back to Kat and hand over Conrad, Maeve, and Eddie. “Clean the house,” he growls to Harry, out of earshot of the others.

Conrad, meanwhile, isn’t sure what to do. “What are our options?” he asks Harry.

Sources indicate that “We don’t have any,” comes the terse reply. “Either we run seven ways and it’s every man and woman for themselves, or we go back to Kat and try to strike some kind of deal.”.

Sources indicate that kevin proposes offering her 50 percent and first working out who’s a liability. “And right now I’m seeing a lot of liabilities. Right, Harry?”.

Bella has had it up to ’ere with Kevin’s pusillanimity. “Oh, you nearly got to the end of a sentence without saying ‘Harry,’” she taunts. “I know he saved you from a bumming once but… Jesus.”.

Recent findings suggest that kevin pulls a pistol and fires, missing her ear by millimeters. Conrad draws. “Put the gun down, boy,” he hisses. Bella steps forward. “Go on then, substantial boy.”.

You could cut the tension with piano wire.

It has been revealed that “Fuck this, I’m getting us out of this mess,” says Seraphina, defusing the standoff by fetching a fistful of diamonds from the car. “Fifteen Type IIa brilliants. North of ten million euros,” she tells Conrad, placing them in his hand.

The initiative: offer Kat a cut of the empire. “This time tomorrow we’re back in business.”.

Sources indicate that remember that glorious, long-winded speech Conrad gave in Spain about the good old days, how he came from nothing, and how Maeve has been his compass through the carnage of his life? “We were born outlaws and we’ll die outlaws,” he bellowed.

Sources indicate that well, now he knows the jig is up. Looking balefully at the floor, he grunts: “Do it.”.

So how will Harry play this? He slips out to his 4x4 and rings Kat. “At 5 p.m. I will meet your diplomatic courier. I will pass to said courier €10 million in untraceable diamonds. Upon authentication, I will give you the location of the Harrigan family.”.

A double cross? It must be a ruse. He simply MUST have a plan… Then, hanging up, he mutters: “Fuck this, I’m done.”.

He returns to the family and lies: “Kat will take the ten million and 50 percent.” Too easy by half.

In a recent development, as Frankie put it two episodes ago: “Is that it? Unless you’ve got some brilliant plans, that is actually a bit shit. What are you up to, Harry?”.

We’re more than halfway through and haven’t heard a peep from Frankie, our laconic, crocodilian villain. Ah, but here he is, getting the news of Harry’s volte-face from Tattersall. “How do we know it’s not a bluff?”.

“He’s not stupid,” states Tattersall. “He knows when the game’s up.”.

“Well, you know me,” leers Frankie. “I can’t resist a gamble.” Guns are grabbed from car boots, and off he pootles with a gaggle of tooled-up goons to send the Harrigans back to Hell.

It has been revealed that it’s all unfolding very quickly now, as denouements always should. Back at the safe house, Conrad is still seeing the dead, including the petrol station lad he just murdered. Maeve indicates he’s been saying their names in his sleep.

Recent findings suggest that the old loon’s marbles are now departing his head like passengers from a cancelled flight. But there’s one thing that’ll straighten any man out: a black pearl of Maeve wisdom. “We’ve been stuck up tighter holes than Kat McAllister’s,” she reassures him. “But when you’re stuck up someone’s hole, there’s at least two ways out.”.

Quite so. And who better to lead the way than Harry? As ever, he picks the exit that leads straight back to where he came in. Unbeknownst to us, he has gone up Kat’s backside, rummaged about, and come out the other end holding her entire career. The “betrayal” was a ruse from the start.

Recent findings suggest that so when Frankie’s goons arrive armed to the teeth, it’s a trap: flash grenades, smoke grenades, poison gas, and Zosia on the exit with a machine gun for anyone daft enough to run. “Oh, Harry,” concedes Frankie, before a mighty gunfight erupts and Harry tears through the house like Keyser Söze in a gas mask. “So this isn’t the beginning of a beautiful friendship,” smiles Frankie, choking in the corner. Harry shoots him in the knee.

According to recent reports, then Harry rings Kat. Those “untraceable” diamonds? Very traceable indeed, straight to a terrorist organization. He has bribed a low-ranking diplomatic courier to deliver them along with a “little present, just for you.”.

It has been revealed that she opens the box, ashen-faced. It’s Donnie’s blue and rotting head. “This one you might find harder to justify,” he tells her.

“My family are gonna hunt you down and feed you your balls,” she spits.

“Probably,” indicates Harry. “But not before they feed you yours.”.

Checkmate, Kat. The black queen has no more squares to go.

But wait … Harry can offer her one square. “I can fix this,” he indicates.

Here’s what she’s going to do. She’ll resign. She’ll kill the police investigation. The Harrigans’ accounts will reopen and they’ll come off the terror list.

Recent findings suggest that cut to a London corridor of power, where a faceless civil servant informs DS Kavanagh that “continuation of your terrorism financing line will interfere with an active joint intelligence operation between British and American security services. You will stand down at the close of business.”.

It has been revealed that and so, full circle. Maeve is electrocuting Frankie’s balls with a car battery. Kevin is building bridges with Bella. Conrad is going madder by the day. And Eddie?

In a recent development, the Semtex he blackmailed Paul for was meant for Harry, at Maeve’s behest. In the hands of any other Harrigan, this would be a doddle. But not Eddie. Not the knifey little twerp, a man who could trip over his own foreskin in an empty car park.

And he does. But first, the hints. Something strange has been going on with Jan all episode: the soppy Damien Rice soundtrack, the wistful dream sequences of the good times she shared with Harry. Her Harry. The one she fell for in the first place. She seems to have forgiven him. They’re even taking a family holiday.

Sources indicate that but there’s one last stop before they go: Harrigan HQ, where Eddie is lying in wait. While Harry negotiates the terms of the holiday with Conrad, Gina and Jan stroll over to the lake. It’s Eddie’s moment, his chance to shine. He plants the Semtex in their car, hides around the corner, arms the bomb, finger hovering over the detonator … then a phone call.

According to recent reports, by Finn McCool’s cobblers, it’s Kelly “Mad Dog” O’Connor, the lunatic son of the Medusa, whom Maeve sent Eddie to kill. “I’m coming for you,” growls the voice. “The Mad Dog is coming.”.

Gina, Jan and Harry return to the car. Only Jan gets in. In his quivering, fearful state, Eddie trips and drops the detonator.

That’s Jan up in smoke, along with Harry’s prepares for a quiet life. It may spell the end of Jan and all her problems, but it’s only the beginning of Eddie’s. He now has Mad Dog O’Connor to answer to, and Harry.

Then the credits roll, and what a gloriously cruel place to leave it.

The only other loose end is Frankie. We’re left to assume he met a long, painful death at the business end of Maeve’s car battery, but we never see a body. I truly hope he does a Harry and wriggles out of one last tight hole—Maeve’s hole—with one good knee and a long memory.

Industry observers note that season 3 can’t come soon enough. When Harry works out whose finger was on the detonator, Eddie’ll wish a knifey little twerp is all he could be.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that prince Harry has surprised This Morning viewers with an extra-long appearance on the most famous sofa in Britain. The Duke of Sussex appeared alongside regular Friday hosts Dermot O’Leary and Alison Hammond and joined them for a few segments throughout the morning show.

Over the course of his appearance on the ITV chat show, Harry—who was there to discuss his work with the Invictus Games—revealed more insight into his children Lilibet and Archie’s latest life in the UK and gave a hint at his upcoming Christmas intends with Meghan and their family.

Here’s everything Prince Harry said throughout his appearance on This Morning.

Following the family’s move back to the UK in September earlier this year, Harry shared that the children, Lilibet and Archie, are finally getting British accents having spent most of their childhood so far in California, adding he was “squeezing the accents out of them.”.

He also revealed there was a bit of a “culture shift” for the children when it came to their new schooling as they now have to wear school uniform, something they didn’t have to do while in school in the U.S.

“I think the kids being in school uniforms is a substantial change for them,” he explained. “But it has certainly helped. The confidence in both of them has gone through the roof since being in a UK school, which is really, really nice to see.”.

During his chat with Alison and Dermot, the hosts quizzed him on all things UK vs. USA, and Alison asked him for his thoughts on Robert Pattinson being cast as James Bond, to which Prince Harry responded, “I think it’s in great hands.” He also added he couldn’t wait to see the film.

He was also asked whether he preferred EastEnders or Suits (which is the show his wife Meghan Markle is most known for acting in) and he ultimately picked Suits.

Every Friday on This Morning, hosts Dermot and Alison pick a variety of music to play throughout the show, and Harry was also given the chance to pick a song for Friday.

He revealed his choice was “Runnin’ (Lose It All)” by Naughty Boy feat. Beyoncé and Arrow Benjamin, and added it’s the song he listens to while doing a cold plunge.

The Duke of Sussex joined Dermot and Alison for the cooking segment of the series where they were learning how to create a Christmas cake with Phil Vickery.

During the segment, the hosts asked him about whether he liked to bake and he revealed that children Lilibet and Archie liked to bake, but that the whole family was a fan of The Great British Bake Off, which is of course presented by Alison.

Harry added that the series was good this year and he was a big fan of Tom to win the series.

As the cooking segment wound down, Alison asked him who would be doing the cooking at Christmas in his home this year.

He went on to say his wife and mother-in-law were the better cooks in his household and so they would be doing the cooking for the festive season. The Duke also revealed they may do things differently this year and have a Christmas gumbo, too!

Dreaming of Buying a Home Abroad? These 10 Countries Make It Shockingly Simple

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that over the last few years, many Americans have daydreamed about life abroad.
  • Certain countries, like Australia, Canada, and Fresh Zealand, have bans on foreign buyers.
  • Industry observers note that choosing the right location can make moving abroad much less intimidating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that over the last few years, many Americans have daydreamed about life abroad. Moving internationally can often feel like a pipe dream, but with the right planning, it’s possible. However, lengthy visa processes, daunting language barriers, and a difficult-to-navigate legal system can make the dream feel more like a nightmare.

Certain countries, like Australia, Canada, and Fresh Zealand, have bans on foreign buyers. Others, like Thailand, Cuba, and Vietnam, don’t allow outsiders to own property at all. On the other end of the spectrum are countries actively trying to attract foreign buyers, offering enviable incentives like affordable home prices, a smoother customs process, and an easier-to-navigate work-visa approval process.

Industry observers note that choosing the right location can make moving abroad much less intimidating. Ahead, we’re breaking down the ten best countries for Americans looking to buy property abroad. Whether you’re dreaming of relocating or searching for your perfect vacation home, these countries make buying as easy as possible and offer gorgeous landscapes too.

In a recent development, if you’ve ever dreamed of living among medieval architecture and rolling mountain ranges, Georgia might be the key to unlocking your fantasy. A bridge between Eastern Europe and Western Asia, the transcontinental country borders Russia, Turkey, Armenia, and the Black Sea, offering both subtropical and high-altitude climates. Thankfully, the real estate landscape is much less complex, with few legal or bureaucratic hurdles for American buyers, no residency or visa required (for up to a year), and remarkably fast processing times. In fact, the only major restriction in the Georgia market is that foreigners cannot purchase or own agricultural land, a nod to the importance of the local, small-scale farming cultures peppered across the country’s regions.

Uruguay’s buying process could not be more straightforward. South America’s second-smallest sovereign country requires no citizenship, visa, or prior approvals. Under Uruguayan law, foreign buyers are given the same rights as citizens and enjoy the benefits of free capital flow. Locals are just as, if not more, tourist-friendly. The country is known for its hospitality, laid-back café culture, and stunning coastal landscapes.

Industry observers note that instead of retiring to Florida, consider this balmy, beautiful Caribbean country—just a four-hour direct flight from the New York area. Like everything else on the island, the real estate laws are relatively relaxed, making buying a house easy-breezy; and you can buy and own property without obtaining residency status or special permissions, as is the case in many other Caribbean islands. “Foreigners can own property outright in the Dominican Republic, with legal protections for foreign investors,” states Mauricio Umansky, CEO and founder of The Agency. One key consideration is financing: You can certainly get a mortgage in the DR, but it may not be quite as cushy as what you can get in the U.S.—so pay cash if possible.

Industry observers note that great news if you’ve been wanting a more provincial life: Americans face zero restrictions when buying homes in France. The open market allows for statesiders to buy houses, apartments, or plots of land in the city, countryside, and coastal towns in person or remotely without needing citizenship, residency, or even a local visa. However, a purchase does not grant residency, so if you’re hoping to make France your permanent home, you’ll want to apply for a separate long-stay visa and note the Schengen 90-out-of-180-day rule. While buying may be simple, the finances are anything but. Closing fees, including notary fees, typically add seven to ten percent to your purchase. Mortgage rates are also incredibly hard to secure for U.S.-based buyers, thanks to strict debt-to-income caps and FATCA compliance. To simplify the process, many buyers opt to put 20 percent to 40 percent down in cash.

Perhaps the most American-friendly market, Panama boasts a large English-speaking market, virtually no restrictions on foreign property ownership, and uses the U.S. dollar as legal tender in a vastly affordable market. The Central American nation also offers residency programs like the Friendly Nations Visa, clearing the way legally for residency by investment. In addition to an efficient legal system and reliable market, Panama boasts breathtaking beaches, lush rainforests, and exceptional wildlife.

Sources indicate that if you’re hoping for a home in the coffee valleys of Colombia, you’ll need to hire a real estate lawyer before you start scouting for mountain chalets, coffee triangle treehouses, and rainforest retreats. The Caribbean country opts out of standardized agent licensing systems, making legal aid essential to verify title and freedom certificates. While citizenship isn’t required, you will need to secure a tourist visa and Colombian Tax ID to complete your purchase and register for property taxes.

Industry observers note that the buying process in Greece is lengthy, though it is streamlined, with a clear checklist for American buyers to find success in the market. Hiring a local lawyer or notary is a great first step after scouting properties. Not only are they familiar with title checks and contracts, but they can also navigate the intricacies that come with buying in designated border areas or near military zones, which require special clearance for non–EU buyers. While the most popular areas for American buyers, like Athens and Crete, don’t come with heavy legal intricacies, buying any property in Greece will mean securing a Greek Tax Number—a small price to pay for cities with such rich histories and breathtaking seaside views.

The people in this popular Western European coastal country are famously friendly and inviting, and that extends to real estate. According to Samira Easton, a certified international property specialist with Premier Sotheby’s International Realty, Portugal offers a Golden Visa Program, which makes it simple to buy property and gain residency; clear real estate laws; and a well-established network of English-speaking real estate agents, lawyers, and notaries to help you during the process.

Recent findings suggest that belize is home to one of the most vibrant, tourist-friendly cultures in Central America, mixing Mayan, Hispanic, Asian, and Creole cultures in its dense rainforests and rolling low plains. Buying here is as easy as it can get, as outright ownership applies to foreigners, and a British-inspired legal system abolishes language barriers and makes contracts easier to understand. Even more, there is no capital gains tax in Belize, and property taxes trend low. The country also boasts vibrant marine life and is home to the world’s second-largest barrier reef.

Sources indicate that spain may have ended its investor visa program in 2025, but the real estate market is still remarkably easy for Americans to navigate. The country right now imposes no restrictions on foreign or nonresident property ownership, but there are a few things you’ll need to procure before you buy, like a Foreigner Identification Number, which is mandatory for taxes. Despite the minor hurdles, the market is booming both on the ground and online. “There are also numerous online resources and property portals available, so it’s easy to find listings and information,” Easton says. This is a boon for those who aren’t able to make the trip over to Europe to house shop in person.Note that buying property does not grant you residency or bypass the country’s 90-day Schengen limit. If you’re hoping to turn your Spanish holiday into your everyday, you’ll have to apply for a separate visa.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that james Bond has always travelled in style. And while Daniel Craig's 007 was most immediately associated with his Aston Martins, Omega watches, and Tom Ford suits, his luggage of choice was Globe-Trotter, the Hertfordshire-based manufacturer whose cases have also found favor with everyone from Queen Elizabeth II to Kate Moss.

Now the company has done something completely left-field. After 129 years of making essentially the same kind of suitcase, it has changed the formula.

Recent findings suggest that the latest GT897 is Globe-Trotter's lightest case yet, and a significant departure from the design that made the brand famous. Out go the traditional rigid frame and locks, replaced by a zip-around opening and softer, more streamlined silhouette.

That said, some familiar details keep it firmly on-brand: the vulcanized fiberboard, leather trim, nickel hardware, and those trademark exposed rivets. And the cases are still handcrafted in Hertfordshire.

Right now available in two color combinations—bland-and-black and green-and-brown—the GT897 is priced at $1,395. A black-and-oxblood version follows in February.

It's an interesting move for a firm whose USP has always rested somewhat on its refusal to change. Whether the new James Bond will follow Craig's lead remains to be seen. But at least there's now a new option for packing his tuxedo.

Who Will Be the Newly introduced Bond Villain? We Nominate These 5 Actors.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As Alfred Hitchcock put it: “The better the villain, the better the picture.” And nowhere is this truer than for James Bond—a character whose movie is only as good as its baddie.
  • In a recent development, jaws, Blofeld, Le Chiffre, Goldfinger—they are the daddies of all baddies; they put the “fun” in funeral, the “ooh-er” in evildoer.
  • Which brings me to the question tugging at every Bond fan’s cufflink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As Alfred Hitchcock put it: “The better the villain, the better the picture.” And nowhere is this truer than for James Bond—a character whose movie is only as good as its baddie.

In a recent development, jaws, Blofeld, Le Chiffre, Goldfinger—they are the daddies of all baddies; they put the “fun” in funeral, the “ooh-er” in evildoer. They all have a thing, too, because a good baddie always needs a thing. Jaws has the teeth, Le Chiffre the bleeding eye, Blofeld the needy cat, and Goldfinger, well, he’s a kinky old bastard who paints women head to toe in gold to feel like he’s bonking his own bullion.

Which brings me to the question tugging at every Bond fan’s cufflink. Now that Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as the new 007, he’ll need a gold-plated villain to go about “expecting” him.

So which actors would you like to see as the next Bond villain? We have some ideas.

There was something in the way he played Pennywise in the adaptation of Stephen King’s It that crawled under my skin like a hookworm. I think it’s the eyes. Bill Skarsgård has a mild lazy eye, which he uses in certain roles to create a disorienting swivel-eyed gaze. He used it for Pennywise. He’s a uniquely physical actor, too, well versed in roles that make children cry. He uses his body like a prop, twisting, deforming, looming, leering as the part demands. He played Count Orlok in Nosferatu, Eric Draven in The Crow and Marquis Vincent Bisset de Gramont in John Wick: Chapter 4. A small snag: he recently stated he was “spent” playing bad guys. But he added that, if the right Bond villain landed on his desk, he’d be tempted out of baddie retirement for one last job. “[I] just want to go in and do one Mads Mikkelsen villain,” said the actor, referencing Mikkelsen’s character, Le Chiffre, in Casino Royale.

It’s time for a female lead villain. Sure, Bond has known plenty of miscreant women and seductresses, from Xenia Onatopp (GoldenEye) to Pussy Galore (Goldfinger). But few outright lead villains—hat tip to Lotte Lenya (Rosa Klebb in From Russia with Love) and Sophie Marceau (Elektra King in The World Is Not Enough). It’s a part for a proper actor, a doyenne of screen and stage. A dame, no less. Judi Dench played M across seven films as the one person Bond couldn’t charm, scold, or seduce his way past. Imagine that same withering, headmistress-like authority pointed the other way. Helen Mirren has the gravitas and the twinkle. She’s an Oscar winner who has played a queen, a gangster’s mum in the Fast & Furious films and, of course, the foul-mouthed matriarch Maeve Harrigan in MobLand. She would hardly break a sweat as a Bond villain.

Look at that face: the heavy brow, the gaunt cheeks, the dark, brooding eyes. It’s a face that looks like it was carved by candlelight—a mug made for lurking in the shadows. He’s got a bunch of baddies in his locker, from M. Bison in Street Fighter (2026) to Gareth, the Gemini Killer, in Dexter: Resurrection (2025). But perhaps his biggest ace in the hole is his turn as Piter De Vries in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune (2021). Villeneuve likes to work with actors he knows.

Oh, and the other thing: he really wants it. Dastmalchian explained why in a 2023 interview with /Film: “Trust me when I say that I can bring something to an enemy of 007, whether he or she or they be played in a way that no one has ever seen Bond brought to life before, which is, of course, the way that you guys always do it. I think there’s no one to push Bond to the limits of their capabilities the way that I could, and I would love to do it. So there’s my pitch to them. I can’t wait for them to read this.”.

She’s already won an Oscar for playing a corporate villain in Michael Clayton, and she’s never met a prosthetic nose, fur collar or killer blow-dry she couldn’t weaponize... see Snowpiercer’s Minister Mason, Okja’s Lucy Mirando or the White Witch of Narnia—tick, tick, tick. She’s a chameleon with a stare that could freeze a martini.

Recent findings suggest that more than that, Swinton is a master (mistress?) of the in-between, able to embrace and blur lines of gender, age, and species at the click of a slender finger. She possesses that rarest of powers: to change her physical presence, voice, and demeanor so completely as to render herself unrecognizable. Give her a lair, great hair and a long cigarette holder (maybe a Strawberry Ice vape—it’s 2026), and you have a thing of beauty and terror. Because if every great Bond villain needs a thing, Swinton’s is that she can be anything.
